en: If fate decrees, let me die,
But let me see where
My valiant mother Kanykei is.
If the cruel enemy Kanchoro
Has laid hands upon my mother,
I shall fight him and spill his blood.
I shall discover the truth.
If I do not return to my lands of Jylgyn and Keң-Kol,
To my renowned Kyrgyz people,
And settle in their dwelling place;
If I do not make my homeland
The ancestral land my father left,
Go and honor his tomb,
And send word to my people—
Ancient Talas and Keң-Koshoy
Are lands left by my forefathers.
He has none of his possessions left,
Nor the gray horse he cherished
In place of an elder brother.
Parted from the gray horse,
Külchoro has no fortune.
Ah, my valiant uncle, may you live;
May Külchoro never know misery.
May God, who creates the soul,
Never visit affliction like this
Upon His mortal servant.
Who has not tilted jauntily
The sable cap upon his head?
While fortune crowned his head,
Who has not gone about in thunderous pride?
When a valiant hero set his purpose,
What enemy before him did not scatter?
I fell captive and grieved,
Parted from my khan and uncle,
Whom I had held most dear.
While my valiant uncle lived,
I towered higher than the hills;
Parted from my hero,
I became more wretched than any man.
My head, once surrounded by followers,
Now reels as I grieve.
By my khan-uncle’s last command,
I have lost the noble steed.
While my fortune remained whole,
Ah, my dear one, I became a burdened soul.
Parted from my uncle,
Having lost the noble gray,
I have camped beside the river.
I have become embers from sobbing,
As though my fire had gone out.
May my gray-maned lord not die;
May Külchoro never know anguish.
We wailed and grieved;
Today we lost the gray.
Stricken and sorrowing,
Parted from the noble gray,
Let me ride in, my whip trailing,
And learn how great his courage is.
I shall hurl harsh words at him
And touch his tender spot.
Glaring in wrath,
If I do not crush him from above
And scatter all his princely pride;
I shall bring misery upon his lord.
If I, Seytek, cannot do so,
May I sink away as though never born,
May I die rather than live.
Kanchoro is the one I seek—
He alone is my sworn enemy.
If he is a lion and a tiger,
And I do not rain shots upon him
Before the five Argali stars set—
My valiant mother Kanykei,
Who nursed me five times over,
From the torments of captivity
And the humiliation of slavery—
If I do not set her free!
If I do not level my flawless spear,
Raise a clamor that splits the earth,
And battle Kanchoro;
If I do not show the enemy
My courage and valor,
My strength and lionheartedness;
If I do not make Khan Bakai master
Of all his vast wealth and herds,
Lead my mother Kanykei
Into her noble palace,
Have myself called Semetey’s son,
And make my valor known to the people;
If I do not wage fierce battle,
And avenge the honor of not one father but seven,
Taking vengeance for my forebears,
May I die as though never created.
Let me see how strong
The fierce and wrathful Külchoro is.
If perfect honor grants me a day,
The Arгын and Kyrgyz, whose names accord,
Are the people my father left me.
Should a cherished khan’s son
Live as a fugitive?
Should a valiant khan’s only son
Live wandering in exile?
I shall bring my people home to Talas
And, unless I die, take vengeance
Upon the swaggering enemy.
I shall show the enemy
My savage, wrathful edge;
I shall go and strengthen
The fury I bear against my foe.
To the vile slave who gorges himself
On frozen goat fat and barren yearling horse,
Drunken with arrogance,
I shall go and send word:
‘Give us now Akolpok, worn on distant campaigns,
And Akkelte, fired in battle.’
I shall demand them
And ask for every possession.
I shall gather what was scattered
And reclaim all that was taken.
If he will not return what was taken,
If he will not heed my words,
If he will not give me the possessions
My father left in trust,
I shall tear open and scatter his bundles
And unleash a dreadful quarrel.
I shall raid his mares from the hills,
Tether his camels from the village,
And vent his rage.
If his savage fury seizes him,
I shall batter his brains to pieces,
And wage such strife.
That utter infidel,
That treacherous Choro warrior,
I shall crush from above
And scatter his full fortune.
Declaring, ‘I am the khan’s son,’
I shall take the road to Chardak,
Test how much strength he has,
Learn how great his power is,
And enter into his vast wealth.
I shall rain shots upon him.
My sorrowful uncle Bakai,
My grandsire left by my father,
My khan whose back is like a mountain,
My elder, like a prophet,
He who wears a blue lynx cap,
The handsomest among all men,
My sacred old man,
My khan and uncle Bakai—
If I do not cross the hills to seek him
And set him free;
If I do not rescue old Bakai, my heirloom,
Whole and unharmed;
If I do not go to Khan Kanchoro
And unleash cold havoc upon the world
For what he will not yield when asked;
If he will not surrender the possessions through counsel,
If I do not seize them without another word!”
So the hero Seytek spoke,
Preparing himself in fury,
Raging like a lion.
His heart surged with many feelings,
And he looked like a lofty blue crag
As he stood before them.
Külchoro, sustained by the patron spirit,
Spoke slowly and firmly,
Beginning his counsel to brave Seytek:
“Ah, you are my beloved, my mainstay,
My lion left by the bloodthirsty hero.
You are the banner fixed upon my spear,
The support of this entrusted life,
A cherished gift cradled in song.
You are the joy before my eyes,
My child Seytek, my good fortune.
When I behold you, my belly is full;
Without you, my cherished one, I have no life.
I shall strike the swaggering, wrathful enemy
Across the nape of his neck;
Even if he has sixty lives,
I shall slaughter him and leave none!
I shall charge in and test
His courage and valor;
I shall divide all his wealth.
With that fiercely wrathful swine
I shall grapple without cease.
If Kanchoro, whom I fight,
Is a warrior and a hero,
A lion who has shaken the world,
Then, if fate decrees, let me die
And let my youthful head behold
The true realm from which none return.
How could I surrender my honor
To that strutting false kinsman?
Boastful Kanchoro,
If your death comes suddenly,
If disaster strikes by chance,
May my perfect mother Aichürök,
Saying, ‘My son died in battle,’
Forgive me through her grief.
For the milk of her white breast,
May my lion mother forgive me.
How could I endure alive
The humiliation he has inflicted?
If I do not repay shame with shame
And relentlessly take my vengeance,
May I sink away as though never born.
He boasts of valor and lionhood,
That consummate, depraved lecher,
Posing as righteous and heroic.
If I do not somehow settle accounts
With cunning Kanchoro,
Going tirelessly upon the road;
If I do not beat the circling madness
Out of that white-deviled swine,
May I die without human honor,
May I sink away as though never born.
Your uncle Külchoro is such a man:
Your support when you climb,
Your prop when you descend;
Your clear road across the hills,
Your countless army when he leads.
My gray fledgling falcon
Would not let a bustard escape the steppe.
I am black steel with a lamb-liver sheen,
Such as no smith could find.
I am your warrior, proven among heroes;
When I lead the first attack,
I am your keen-eyed Choro of old.
Not merely keen-eyed Külchoro—
I am one tested by many nations.
If you thrust me against a stubborn foe,
I am a sharp, steel-headed spear,
Aimed exactly where you intend.
If you unleash me upon the chosen foe,
I am a dark, double-edged blade.
I am Külchoro indeed,
The renowned lion and tiger
Who crushes the foe he faces.
Set the dawn as our appointed time
And take your uncle Kül as companion.
I shall teach you what you do not know,
And knowingly lead you against the foe.
I shall be a banner to your kin;
If you unleash me upon your enemy,
I shall be a singular black poison
That bursts lungs and spills gall.
While your tiger father lived,
He would wreak utter slaughter
Upon the Chinese encamped on the heights.
If I was left afoot in dangerous ground,
Your precious gray-maned lion of a father
Would take me up behind him.
He never said, ‘There is no room behind me,’
Nor, ‘Let this poor wretch
Stay safely behind to tend the horses.’
I possessed the strength for battle.
